1.title: Study strategy and the role of practice
elements: para
Active engagement with material. Taking notes on the code is recommended for future reference
para

Practice as the key to programming. He advised reading problem sets as soon as they appear so terminology sinks in, and using lectures to reinforce unfamiliar words. He also reassured students that running Anaconda and typing commands cannot damage their computer, encouraging them not to be afraid of breaking it
para
Three core outcomes. He noted that these outcomes are reinforced by lectures, examples, and tests, and that practice underlies all of them
para
Importance of practice. Practice is presented as the foundation for achieving all three outcomes; students must type code regularly and work on many problems to succeed
para

Objects and data structures. Learning how to program involves deciding which objects to create and how to represent knowledge with data structures, which is the broad term for organizing information in a program
para
Control flow. Programs are not purely linear; they include control flow that allows decisions and jumps, enabling the program to react to different conditions
para
Readability and modularity. Writing readable code means organizing it so that others in a company or your future self can understand it, which requires modular, well‑structured design
para
Long‑term maintainability. Readable and well‑organized code lets you revisit problem sets later and understand what you were doing, avoiding the difficulty of deciphering a messy codebase
para

Basic computer actions. A computer performs calculations and stores the results in memory; modern machines can execute about a billion calculations per second and have hundreds of gigabytes of storage
para

Primitive vs. user‑defined calculations. Computers support two kinds of calculations: built‑in primitive operations such as addition, subtraction, and multiplication, and user‑defined calculations created by combining these primitives
para
Creating custom calculations. Once a language provides primitive calculation types, a programmer can combine them to define new, custom calculations that extend the language's capabilities

question.q: What does the lecturer suggest new programmers should do to become better at coding?
question.answer: Practice regularly, read problem sets early, and follow along with in‑class coding exercises.

elements: u0e0
Course Intro. The session will cover basic administrative details and an overview of computation, explaining what computers do at a high level
u1e0

Python Basics. We will start with Python basics, covering mathematical operations that can be performed in Python. The slides and code for these topics will be available before the lecture, so students should download them. In‑class exercises will be provided on the slides and are encouraged to be completed during class
u1e1
Study Strategy. During lectures, recalling terms from the problem sets helps solidify understanding. Practice is emphasized as the key to mastering programming, similar to math or reading
u2e0
Practice First. Fear of breaking the computer is unfounded; running Anaconda and typing commands will not harm the system
u2e1

Course Roadmap. The course is structured around three core outcomes: knowledge of concepts, programming skills, and problem‑solving ability. These are reinforced through lectures, examples, and problem sets, with practice underpinning all three
u3e0

Learning to Program. Learning how to program involves deciding which objects to create and how to represent knowledge with data structures. Programs are not linear; they include control flow that allows decisions and jumps
u3e1

Readable Code. Writing readable code means organizing it so that others in a company or future you can understand it. Code should be modular, well‑structured, and easy to read, enabling others to use or revisit it later
u4e0

Computer Function. A computer performs calculations and stores the results in memory. Modern machines can execute on the order of a billion calculations per second. They also have large storage capacities, often measured in hundreds of gigabytes
u5e0

Primitive Calculation Types. Computers perform two kinds of calculations: built‑in operations and user‑defined operations. Built‑in operations are low‑level primitives such as addition, subtraction, and multiplication. Once a language supplies these primitives, a programmer can combine them to create more complex, custom calculations
u5e1
Custom Calculations. By combining primitive types, a programmer can define new calculations, effectively creating a new type of operation that the language does not provide natively
